posts.cooked:
For stores with suppliers that take 3+ weeks, how do you decide when to reorder? Do you go by a set number of days of stock, a minimum quantity, or gut feel? And has a supplier ever been late enough that you sold out anyway?

I’m asking because I build a reorder app and I want to get this part right for people with slow suppliers. Curious how others handle it.
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

Days of cover works better than a fixed minimum once lead times get long, because a min that’s fine in a slow month is too low in a busy one. With a 3+ week supplier I’d set it up like this:

Reorder point = average daily sales × (lead time in days + days between your orders) + safety stock. Use the last 30 to 60 days of sales rather than the whole year so seasonality shows up.

For safety stock, go by how late that supplier has actually been, not what they quote. If they say 21 days but your last few POs landed in 28 to 35, plan on 30 and hold about a week of extra stock on top.

And yes, late suppliers sell people out all the time. What helps most is logging quoted vs actual arrival for every PO and updating each supplier’s lead time every few orders.
This post was flagged by the community and is temporarily hidden.

One thing I’d add to what’s already here: I don’t use one reorder point for a whole product. Different colors of the same style can move at really different speeds, so the number has to sit on the variant. A fixed minimum burned me on that — a slow color still looked fine while the popular one was already too late to catch.

And for lead time, I use the actual average from PO sent to units being sellable, not the factory’s quoted production time. Door to door is usually longer once you count packing, freight, and the odd customs hold.

One thing I’d add to the formula answers: with a slow supplier, how often you order matters as much as the lead time. If you place one order every six weeks with a four-week supplier, each order has to cover about ten weeks of sales, so a late shipment hurts twice as much. Ordering a bit more often, in smaller lots, usually cuts the stockout risk more than extra safety stock does.

For the “late enough that I sold out anyway” case, I’d decide the fallback in advance: which top few sellers you’d pay to air freight or split off a smaller rush order, and whether you’d switch the product to preorder instead of letting it show sold out. Deciding that while it’s calm is much easier than during a stockout.

And take the slowest of the last 3 to 5 deliveries as your lead time, not the average.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
For suppliers with lead times of three weeks or more, participants recommend basing reorder decisions on expected demand during replenishment—not relying on a fixed minimum or gut feel. One suggested formula is average daily sales multiplied by supplier lead time plus the interval between orders, with safety stock added. Recent sales (roughly 30–60 days) can better reflect current demand, while actual delivery records should replace supplier estimates when calculating lead times.

Several details affect the calculation: set reorder points for each product variant, since colors or sizes may sell at different rates, and include the full time from placing an order until stock is sellable. Ordering smaller quantities more frequently may reduce risk, especially when orders are otherwise spaced far apart. For protection against unreliable suppliers, suggestions include using the slowest of the last few deliveries, tracking quoted versus actual arrival dates, and planning fallback options such as air freight, rush orders, or preorders for top sellers. No single policy was adopted; the discussion offers practical guidance, while the appropriate thresholds remain dependent on each store’s sales and supplier history.
